subject: Culture
title: Passover's Story
description: A micro-lesson that makes Passover's Story usable.

hook.text: Every Passover, Jewish families retell the exodus from Egypt as if they themselves just escaped.

buildup.text: The Seder meal uses symbolic foods: bitter herbs for suffering, unleavened bread for haste.

discovery.text: Passover may be the world's oldest continuously celebrated religious festival—over 3,000 years running.

twist.text: Historians debate whether the Exodus happened as described. The festival's power doesn't depend on literal truth.

climax.text: Passover teaches that freedom is never guaranteed. Each generation must remember the cost of liberty.

punchline.text: They retell the story so they never forget it.

quiz.question: What do bitter herbs symbolize at the Passover Seder?

details.summary: Passover (Pesach) commemorates the Israelites' exodus from Egyptian slavery — a founding narrative of Jewish identity retold every year through the Seder meal. For over 3,000 years, this festival has kept the memory of liberation alive, inspiring freedom movements worldwide.
details.whyItMatters: Passover's liberation narrative influenced the American civil rights movement, anti-apartheid activism, and liberation theology globally. Its annual retelling shows how festivals preserve revolutionary memory across millennia.
takeaways: Passover commemorates the Israelites' escape from Egyptian slavery
The Seder meal retells the Exodus story through ritual foods
Matzah (unleavened bread) recalls the haste of the escape

faq.question: What happens during a Passover Seder?
faq.answer: The Seder follows a specific order (seder means order) using the Haggadah text. Ritual foods represent aspects of slavery and freedom — bitter herbs for suffering, charoset for mortar, matzah for the rushed escape.

faq.question: How has Passover influenced other freedom movements?
faq.answer: African American spirituals drew heavily on Exodus imagery — 'Go Down Moses' and 'Let My People Go.' Martin Luther King Jr. frequently invoked the Passover narrative. Liberation theologians in Latin America used it to frame their struggles.
